Title: Investigation of pairing correlations on computed Gamow-Teller strength distributions and associated -decay half-lives
Abstract: We investigate the eﬀect of pairing correlations on the computed Gamow-Teller
(GT) strength distributions and corresponding β-decay half-lives. The calcula-
tions are performed for a total of 47 sd-shell nuclei, for 20 < A < 30, employing
the pn-QRPA model. Our calculations use three diﬀerent values of pairing gaps
computed using three diﬀerent empirical formulae.
The GT strength distri-
bution and centroid values change considerably with change in the pairing gap
values. This in turn leads to diﬀerences in computed half-lives. The pairing gaps
computed using the mass dependent formula result in the calculated half-lives
in better agreement with the measured data.
Keywords:
Gamow-Teller strength distribution, pn-QRPA, Pairing
correlation, Half-lives, Electron capture, β-decay, Ikeda sum rule
1. Introduction
Core-collapse supernovae are considered to be one of the main contributors
to the formation of heavier elements in the stellar matter. Weak interactions
processes, especially electron capture (ec) and β-decay (bd), are believed to
control both lepton to baryon fraction (Ye) and entropy of the stellar core and
play a major role leading to the core-collapse of the massive stars [1, 2]. The ec
eﬀectively reduces the number of electrons that provide the pressure support,

while bd has a converse action. Both these processes have a direct inﬂuence on
the overall Ye ratio of the core of the star. These weak interaction processes are
important, not only in the accurate determination of the structure of the stel-
lar core, but also play a vital role in the elemental abundance calculation and
nucleosynthesis. The computation of these reactions under stelalr conditions
largely depend on the accurate and reliable calculation of Gamow-Teller (GT)
response of the nuclei [2].
The GT transitions are the most common spin–isospin (στ) type weak interac-
tion processes in atomic nuclei [3]. In spherical coordinate system, the isospin
has three components, τ+, τ−and τ0. The τ+ corresponds to the GT transitions
(GT+) in β+ or ec direction, where conversion of proton to neutron takes place.
The τ−represents the GT−transition where a neutron is changed to a proton
via β−decay. The component τ0 refers to inelastic neutrino-nucleus scattering
for low neutrino energies. At start of core-collapse, due to low densities (∼1010
g/cm3) and temperatures (300 - 800 keV), the chemical potential of electrons
and nuclear Q-value have comparable magnitudes. Under such scenario, the ec
rates are sensitive to the detailed description of the GT strength distributions.
However at much higher core densities, once the chemical potential exceeds the
Q-value, the ec rates are governed by the total GT strength and centroid values.
Therefore, a detailed knowledge of the GT distributions is in order for a reliable
computation of stellar weak rates and β-decay half-lives.
The GT transitions can be extracted, experimentally, via diﬀerent charge-exchange
reactions e.g.
(p, n) [4], (n, p) [5], (3He, t) [6] and (t, 3He) [7].
The GT
strength distributions of hundreds of unstable nuclei are required for modeling
and simualtion of core-collapse supernovae. A nuclear model, preferably micro-
scopic in nature, is required that can reliably calculate GT strength distributions
and associated β-deacy half-lifes in reasonable agreement with the available ex-
perimental data. Several attempts have been made in the past to investigate
the β-decay properties. Few noticeable mentions are the computations based
on gross theory [8], QRPA e.g. ([9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14]) and shell model ([15]).
The gross theory calculations are unable to provide details of nuclear structure
of individual nuclei and adopt a statistical approach to determine the β-decay
properties. The shell model and pn-QRPA are the two microscopic approaches,
widely employed for the accurate and reliable computations of the β-decay half-
lives and stellar weak rates. However, the former approach use the Brink-Axel
hypothesis [16] to include the contribution of excited state GT strength dis-
tributions at high temperature. The pn-QRPA model can compute the exited
state GT transitions without invoking the hypothesis.
Pairing of nucleons inside the nucleus is treated using the BCS approach. The
value of the pairing gaps is one of the crucial parameters used in the pn-QRPA
model [9, 10]. In this study, we investigate the eﬀect of pairing gaps on the
computed GT strength distributions and β-decay half-lives. We calculated the
half-lives of 47 sd-nuclei with mass in the range 20 < A < 30, employing the
pn-QRPA model. The pairing gaps were calculated using three diﬀerent empir-
ical formulae, to be discussed in the next section. The computed half-lives were
then compared with experimental data [17].
2

The paper is structured as follows. Section 2 provides a brief overview of the
formalism used in our calculation. Section 3 discusses our results. The ﬁnal
section contains summary and concluding remarks.

3. Results and Discussion
In this work, we used the pn-QRPA model to investigate the impact of pair-
ing gaps on the computed GT strength and β-decay half-lives. We performed
the calculations for a total of 47 sd-shell nuclei with masses in the range 20 <
A < 30, employing the three diﬀerent schemes of pairing gaps denoted by TF,
3TF and 5TF, as discussed in the previous section. Out of these 47 cases, 32
decay by electron emission (β−) while 15 are unstable to positron emission (β+
decay). We also compare our computed half-lives with the experimental data
taken from Ref. [17], referred to as Aud17 here onwards.
Fig. 1 shows the computed GT strength distributions for the three selected β−
cases, 29Al, 27Ne and 22F, employing the three diﬀerent schemes of pairing gaps.
It can be seen that the strength distributions change considerably once the value
of the pairing gap is changed. For the case 29Al, the strength distributions us-
ing TF and 3TF formulae are more or less the same. However, the strength
changes considerably for 5TF scheme. The strength for the cases 27Ne and 22F
do changes for all the three schemes. Fig. 2 depicts similar results for the β+
cases 23Al, 20Na and 21Mg. It is to be noted that only the strength within the
Qβ−/β+ window has been shown is these two ﬁgures.
Table 1 displays the computed pairing gaps and half-lives using the three diﬀer-
ent formulae for the β−cases, whereas Table 2 shows the corresponding results
for the β+ cases. The computed half-lives are compared with the experimental
data of Aud17, shown in the last column of these tables. It can be seen that
the computed half-lives using the three formulae are in decent comparison for
cases such as 20O, 24,26,29Ne and 28,30Mg. However, signiﬁcant diﬀerence in the
computed half-lives were noted for some other cases e.g. 23,26F, 27Ne, 25Na and
27P. In comparison with Aud17, the TF computed half-lives are in overall better
agreement. The calculated half-lives using TF scheme were in comparison with
Aud17, within 100% deviation for 29 cases, within 500% for 13 cases and the
rest of the cases fall within 1000% deviation. Similarly, the computed half-lives
using 3TF (5TF) scheme were in agreement with Aud17, within 100% for 24
(24) cases, within 500% for 8 (7) cases, 1 (3) cases lies within 1000% and the rest
were above 1000% deviation. Our study suggests that the computed half-lives
are altered by the choice of pairing gaps. The reasons behind the diﬀerences in
computed half-lives with diﬀerent pairing gap values may be traced to the GT
strength distributions and centroid values which we discuss next.
Table 3 and Table 4 display the GT centroid values for the β− and β+ cases
respectively. The GT centroid values change with the pairing gaps. For the β−
cases, the centroid using TF is more or less the same as 3TF, but 5TF gives
higher centroid values. For the β+ cases, the centroid values using TF, 3TF and
5TF are all quite diﬀerent. The reason behind the diﬀerence in centroid is the
change in the GT strength distribution. The GT centroid is the weighted average
of the centroids of the excited states, weighted by the GT strength in those states.
As such, when the GT strength distribution changes, the centroid value also changes.
In the case of β−, the GT strength is mostly in the ground state, so a slight change
in the ground state centroid can lead to the change in the overall centroid. But in
the case of β+ which involves transitions to higher excited states, the change in the
GT strength distribution can have a more pronounced impact on the centroid.
6

We have also computed the GT strength for all 47 cases. The GT strength for
β− and β+ cases are shown in Figs. 3 and 4 respectively. The GT strength
for β− cases is higher for all the three pairing gap schemes. The strength for
β+ cases is generally lower, except for some cases like 26F, 27Ne, 25Na and
27P. The overall GT strength is a function of the pairing gap, and the pairing
gap is inversely proportional to the square root of the mass for the TF scheme.
As a result, the pairing gap is larger for lighter nuclei and smaller for heavier
nuclei. This leads to a higher GT strength for lighter nuclei, as their pairing gaps
are larger, meaning more pairing, leading to more strength in the GT transitions.
For the β− cases, the GT strength is higher, which aligns with the expectation that
pairing enhances the GT strength. The GT strength for β+ cases is lower because
the pairing is less prominent in heavier nuclei, leading to less GT strength.
The comparison of the computed half-lives with experimental data in Tables 1 and
2 shows that the half-lives using the TF pairing gap are in the better agreement
with the experimental data. The half-lives using 3TF and 5TF are sometimes
in a much worse agreement. For instance, for the β− cases, the computed half-lives
using 3TF and 5TF are sometimes by a factor of 2 to 10 higher or lower than
the experimental values. Similarly, for the β+ cases, the half-lives computed using
the three pairing gap schemes show a variation, with the 5TF scheme sometimes
giving half-lives that are much lower than the experimental data. This suggests that
the choice of the pairing gap formulae can significantly affect the computed half-lives,
and thus the model's ability to reproduce experimental data. The reason behind
this is the interplay between the pairing gaps and the GT strength distributions,
as discussed earlier.
The impact of pairing on the GT strength and centroid can be understood by
looking at the results. The pairing gap is a measure of the strength of the pairing
force, and a larger pairing gap implies more pairing, which would lead to more
strength in the GT transitions. The centroid is the average energy of the excited
states, and a higher centroid implies that the GT transitions are to higher energy
states. The pairing gap and centroid are both crucial in determining the β-decay
half-lives. The half-life is inversely proportional to the sum of the GT strengths
weighted by the phase space factors. Therefore, an increase in the GT strength
and centroid would lead to a decrease in the half-life, and vice versa.
The three diﬀerent pairing gap formulae used in the study have varying
dependencies on the nuclear mass. The TF formula is mass-dependent and decreases
with increasing mass, while the 3TF and 5TF formulae have more complex dependencies
on the nuclear mass and the separation energies. The 5TF formula, which
depends on both the proton and neutron separation energies, is more sensitive
to the changes in the nuclear mass and deformation. The binding energies used
in the 5TF formula are from the mass compilation of Audi et al. [25], which
provides a more accurate description of the nuclear structure.

3. Results and Discussion
In this work, we used the pn-QRPA model to investigate the impact of pair-
ing gaps on the computed GT strength and β-decay half-lives. We performed
the calculations for a total of 47 sd-shell nuclei with masses in the range 20 <
A < 30, employing the three diﬀerent schemes of pairing gaps denoted by TF,
3TF and 5TF, as discussed in the previous section. Out of these 47 cases, 32
decay by electron emission (β−) while 15 are unstable to positron emission (β+
decay). We also compare our computed half-lives with the experimental data
taken from Ref. [17], referred to as Aud17 here onwards.
Fig. 1 shows the computed GT strength distributions for the three selected β−
cases, 29Al, 27Ne and 22F, employing the three diﬀerent schemes of pairing gaps.
It can be seen that the strength distributions change considerably once the value
of the pairing gap is changed. For the case 29Al, the strength distributions us-
ing TF and 3TF formulae are more or less the same. However, the strength
changes considerably for 5TF scheme. The strength for the cases 27Ne and 22F
do changes for all the three schemes. Fig. 2 depicts similar results for the β+
cases 23Al, 20Na and 21Mg. It is to be noted that only the strength within the
Qβ−/β+ window has been shown is these two ﬁgures.
Table 1 displays the computed pairing gaps and half-lives using the three diﬀer-
ent formulae for the β−cases, whereas Table 2 shows the corresponding results
for the β+ cases. The computed half-lives are compared with the experimental
data of Aud17, shown in the last column of these tables. It can be seen that
the computed half-lives using the three formulae are in decent comparison for
cases such as 20O, 24,26,29Ne and 28,30Mg. However, signiﬁcant diﬀerence in the
computed half-lives were noted for some other cases e.g. 23,26F, 27Ne, 25Na and
27P. In comparison with Aud17, the TF computed half-lives are in overall better
agreement. The calculated half-lives using TF scheme were in comparison with
Aud17, within 100% deviation for 29 cases, within 500% for 13 cases and the
rest of the cases fall within 1000% deviation. Similarly, the computed half-lives
using 3TF (5TF) scheme were in agreement with Aud17, within 100% for 24
(24) cases, within 500% for 8 (7) cases, 1 (3) cases lies within 1000% and the rest
were above 1000% deviation. Our study suggests that the computed half-lives
are altered by the choice of pairing gaps. The reasons behind the diﬀerences in
computed half-lives with diﬀerent pairing gap values may be traced to the GT
strength distributions and centroid values which we discuss next.
Table 3 and Table 4 display the values of total GT strength and energy cen-
troid of the computed GT strength distributions employing the three schemes
of pairing gaps for the β−and β+ decays, respectively. The cut-oﬀenergy in
daughter is also shown, in the last column of these two tables.
The cut-oﬀ
value lies within Qβ window (see column 2 of Table 3 & 4). It can be seen that
changing the value of pairing gap slightly alter the total strength for most of the
cases. However, at times, the total strength is signiﬁcantly increased/decreased
with change in the △nn(△pp) values. For example, the total strength for 27Ne
computed using the 5TF scheme is signiﬁcantly smaller than those computed
using TF and 3TF schemes. Similarly, the total strength for 22,23F using the
6

TF scheme is considerably bigger than the one calculated using 3TF scheme.
Similar diﬀerence were found in the centroid values. The smaller total strength
value of 27Ne using 5TF leads to smaller weak rate and correspondingly higher
computed half life as compare to the other two schemes (see Table 1). In the
same way, the higher strength values of 22,23F using TF leads to smaller half-
lives.
The re-distribution of GT strength is another factor which eﬀect the
computed centroids and half life values. At times the GT strength shifts to
higher excitation energy than cut-oﬀvalue shown in the last column of Table 3
& 4. For 25Na, the 3TF scheme places the centroid value at considerably higher
excitation energy than TF and 5TF schemes. This leads to very smaller rate
and correspondingly very high computed half life (Table 1). Similar trend were
found for the other cases as well.

4. Summary and Conclusion
We presented the calculation of GT strength distributions and β-decay half-
lives for a total of 47 sd-shell nuclei in the mass range 20 < A < 30 employing
the pn-QRPA model. Three diﬀerent formulae were used to compute the pairing
gaps between the nucleons in order to investigate their eﬀect on the calculated
GT strength distributions and half-lives. The GT strength distributions and
centroids were altered, in few cases, substantially, with change in pairing gap
values.
The β-decay half-lives computed using the mass dependent formula
(TF) were in overall better comparison with the measured data. For few cases,
studied in this project, 3TF and 5TF formulae for pairing gaps reproduced the
measured half-lives the best.
